summary:
Greater Poland Voivodeship stands under Poland's national framework, and the sources document no voivodeship-specific deviation from it. The findings below are national standards as they apply to a visitor in this province.

Detention is the clearest documented risk to a trans visitor. On 13 March 2024 the Association for Legal Intervention reported that a Polish regional court placed a transgender Vietnamese woman, on hormone therapy since 2018, in a guarded centre for male foreign nationals. Polish law bars placement wherever a stay would threaten life or health or the person shows signs of having suffered violence; the Border Guard refused to move or release her regardless, and she was freed only after the association applied to the Border Guard Post commander. The case report sets the framework applied to trans foreigners in immigration detention here.

Courts have proved willing to intervene. On 11 July 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found that Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 of the Convention by denying a trans woman hormone-replacement therapy in Siedlce prison, awarding EUR 8,000 in damages. The Court left the alleged Articles 3 and 14 breaches undecided but held that the refusal had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate. The judgment binds Poland as a whole and governs healthcare for trans people in Polish custody in every province, including this one. Poland operates no specialised trans prison section, so placement decisions remain individual and unpredictable.

Entry itself is straightforward for many nationalities: Global Affairs Canada's travel advisory records visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days. The same advisory lists sexual orientation among reported motives for harassment in Poland, alongside physical appearance and foreigner status.

The wider legal environment is in transition. Human Rights Watch describes LGBT-rights reform under the Prime Minister Tusk government as slow and insufficient through 2024. Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; a March draft Penal Code amendment raising penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech and violence cleared the Government Legislation Centre in May before approval was postponed, and a second bill followed in late October 2024. The Prosecutor General established a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.
tangentialFactors:
Recognition of same-sex relationships has moved materially. In June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the directive issued by his predecessor Ziobro that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September 2024 the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Poland's absence of partnership recognition leaves couples in an illegal contrary to their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

The ECtHR's 11 July 2024 judgment rejected the Article 3 claim alongside the Article 8 win, so a visitor cannot assume that medication denial in Polish custody will be litigated successfully on inhuman-treatment grounds; the successful route documented is Article 8.

The detention case and the prison ruling arise from different custody systems, immigration detention and penal custody, but both turn on the same failure: medication and placement decisions taken without regard to a trans person's documented treatment history.
localsOnly:
Polish law bars placing a detained person where the stay would threaten life or health or where the person shows signs of having suffered violence. The Association for Legal Intervention's application to the Border Guard Post commander secured release in the March 2024 case, indicating that formal application to the border agency commander remains an available route for residents as well as visitors.

The ECtHR judgment of 11 July 2024 is binding on Poland, and its finding that denial of hormone-replacement therapy had no reasonable legal grounds and was disproportionate sets the standard for healthcare in Polish prisons and detention facilities nationwide.

Residents in this province are covered by the same national framework on hate-speech protection and partnership recognition that applies to visitors; the announced extension of hate-speech protection to gender identity and the pending partnership-recognition framework remain subject to legislative completion.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the March and October 2024 hate-speech bills at the time of travel is unresolved in these sources; the inventory records passage through the Government Legislation Centre and postponement of approval, not final enactment, and no later legislative outcome is sourced here.

Whether the ECtHR judgment has been implemented in Polish prison regulations, and whether any specialised placement policy for trans detainees now exists, is not sourced in this inventory.

No voivodeship-specific data on Greater Poland's own detention facilities, their trans-inmate placement practice, or local hate-crime reporting rates is available in the sources reviewed; the province-level picture rests on the national framework.

Whether the announced special Prosecutor General response team has issued guidelines specifically addressing anti-trans violence, as distinct from anti-LGBTI violence generally, is not resolved in these sources.
